name: Tomas Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a power-line repair crew on the older streets near the east yard, where one bad connector can darken a row of homes. I earned a two-year technical diploma and have become the person sent to stubborn faults; I'm 43 now. Restoring a street's power is satisfying, but storm shifts take me away from family meals.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and how do you handle new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a school nurse, and our two children are still in school. My lineworker pay is above the usual rate, the mortgage is manageable, we have about nine months of expenses saved and plenty of other utilities nearby. I help at our union branch, but I have never used an AI tool; I prefer a meter reading and a signed work order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a faster office form is fine if it gets us to the fault sooner. The power still comes back because a lineworker checks the connector and fixes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead job looks sound, and my partner's school nursing work is steady. We have about nine months of expenses saved, a mortgage we can manage and several other utility crews nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the old-neighbourhood repair rota and give the apprentices the same hands-on tests. At the next union branch meeting I'll bring up a simple rule: any changed work order must still name the person who checked the isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for our household. I would be pleased if the office lost some repetitive typing without changing the safe repair work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the apprentice do before touching a connector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a street outage I ask the apprentice to point to the open switch and read the tester before touching a damaged connector. A short power-line work order cannot stand in for an open switch and a tester reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask the union branch to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The meeting is about a named safety check, not a campaign against every computer. I would ask the branch to put it in the next workplace safety discussion.

say: **Faster forms** are useful when they still name the person checking isolation.
A **damaged connector** needs a trained lineworker and an actual tester reading.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and nearby utility crews make my own income feel secure.
I would welcome less **routine typing** for the office without changing field safety.
do: **Keep** the neighbourhood repair rota and physical apprentice tests.
**Raise** named isolation checks at the next union branch safety meeting.
feel: **Calm** about work and money, with steady attention to safety.
S0.quote: A short power-line work order cannot stand in for an open switch and a tester reading.
fieldNote: He is already active in a **union branch** and makes a specific safety request.
Strong savings and several nearby crews explain **household calm** in this mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep neighbourhood repair rota and apprentice isolation tests
Raise named isolation checks at union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may buy fittings and answer calls faster, but no planner should decide a crew can skip a safety pause. The company should show workers how the new schedules affect hours before it changes the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair work is mostly hands-on, yet a smaller planning office might push more checks onto crew leads. I can find another line employer if necessary, but I'd rather bargain over paid checking time here than start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll gather six weeks of callout rosters and compare them with the new software schedule if it arrives. At the union safety committee I'll ask for paid time to verify isolation plans and for a stop-work rule when the machine's directions disagree with the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about workload and younger colleagues, though my own wage still looks fairly safe. I do not want an apprentice blamed for a plan nobody had time to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the plan conflicts with the pole?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the repair and call control before we climb. The committee needs a rule saying that pause is paid work, so the crew isn't punished for doing it. A power-line safety pause should be paid work, not a fault charged to the apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you take to the committee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the six-week roster comparison, the employer's proposed checking time and a written response. If hours haven't changed, we'd still insist on the stop rule because safety isn't only a wage issue.

say: **AI schedules** must allow paid safety pauses when the site differs from the plan.
The company should publish **roster effects** before changing callout work.
think: My **hands-on repair role** looks safer than office planning work.
A smaller planning team could shift **unpaid checking** onto crew leads and apprentices.
do: **Compare** six weeks of callout rosters with the new schedule if introduced.
**Ask** the union safety committee for paid checks and a written stop-work rule.
feel: **Uneasy** about shifted work and blame, with my own wage still fairly secure.
S1.quote: A power-line safety pause should be paid work, not a fault charged to the apprentice.
fieldNote: He seeks **written roster evidence** and a safety rule through an existing committee.
The concern is **responsibility shifting** to crews even if his own job remains.

steps.text: Compare six weeks of callout rosters if software schedule arrives
Ask union safety committee for paid checks and stop-work rule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 changes the dispatch desk before capable field robots arrive around 2031. We need a written crew plan and a say in any robot safety trial, not a promise that everybody will become a supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nine months saved gives my family time, and there are other line employers nearby. Still, a capable repair robot could cut our crew's ordinary hours, and my partner's school nursing job cannot carry the whole mortgage by itself. My family has nine months of savings; that time does not make a lost power-line wage harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the union branch to call a meeting with the electricity company on 2028 dispatch staffing and 2031 field crews. We'll agree household spending limits before buying another vehicle, and if my hours are formally cut I will apply to an open line job nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possible cut, but I can still make a plan. I would lose sleep over an actual roster change, not the bare date on this card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children we have savings and I am asking questions at work. I would not tell them their school nurse parent must suddenly support us alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply to another line employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for an open lineworker post after a formal cut, not leave a good wage on a guess. If the company offers paid safety training tied to an actual crew role, I will consider it with the branch.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches dispatch before capable line robots arrive around 2031.
Workers need a written **field crew plan** and a voice in robot safety trials.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** gives us time, but cannot replace a full lineworker wage indefinitely.
A robot could reduce **ordinary crew hours**, despite the number of nearby employers.
do: **Join** a union meeting with management on 2028 dispatch and 2031 crews.
**Delay** another vehicle purchase until household spending limits are agreed.
**Apply** to a nearby open line post if a formal hours cut occurs.
feel: **Anxious** about possible crew-hour cuts, with savings and local options.
S2.quote: My family has nine months of savings; that time does not make a lost power-line wage harmless.
fieldNote: His savings support **deliberate collective action** rather than a rushed exit.
He treats a job move as **conditional** on a formal hours cut and an actual opening.
He does not claim that a **training enquiry** is enrolment.

steps.text: Join union meeting with management on dispatch and field crews
Delay another vehicle purchase until spending limits agreed
Apply to nearby open line post if hours formally cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a chance to put robots through actual storm repairs before 2034. Thinking AI by 2031 may change dispatch first, so the field crew should keep the right to reject a plan that ignores the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could probably move among local utilities if this one cuts teams, but I want the apprentices coming behind us to have real repair hours. A robot pilot that takes all the easier calls could hollow out training even before jobs disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union training committee to count apprentice repair hours each quarter. If the company runs a robot pilot, I'll request a paid crew observer and a rule that apprentices still practise isolation and connector work on real jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the next generation more than my own mortgage. Our nine-month reserve and nearby employers give my household some room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What apprentice hours would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count actual pole and connector jobs, not just classroom hours. An apprentice who only watches a line-repair robot will not be ready when a storm jams it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a pilot agreement need to contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pilot agreement should state paid observer hours and a minimum of supervised apprentice field jobs. I'd bring those numbers back to the branch and ask members to vote on the proposal.

say: **Storm trials** should test robots before 2034 field deployment, with a worker able to stop the job.
**Apprentice field hours** need protection as thinking AI changes dispatch by 2031.
think: My own **mortgage** has some buffer and other nearby employers.
A pilot might strip **entry repair work** from apprentices before it cuts full jobs.
do: **Count** apprentice pole and connector jobs each quarter through the union committee.
**Request** paid observers and supervised field hours in the robot pilot agreement.
feel: **Uneasy** about apprentice training, while my household has some room.
S3.quote: An apprentice who only watches a line-repair robot will not be ready when a storm jams it.
fieldNote: He targets **apprentice practice** and paid observation rather than claiming to learn robot controls himself.
The union action has **specific measures**: field jobs, observer hours and a branch vote.

steps.text: Count apprentice pole and connector jobs through union committee quarterly
Request paid observers and field hours in robot pilot agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us negotiate a proper path for lineworkers and apprentices before capable field robots arrive around 2039. Thinking AI in 2036 changes the office first; the company should not treat that as permission to cut safe field training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 56 I may prefer teaching in the yard to climbing after a storm, but only a full paid instructor vacancy would make that possible. We have about nine months saved and a mortgage, so I can wait for a genuine offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my line safety tickets current and continue the union training committee's annual review of apprentice field hours. If a full-wage instructor position with real practice opens, I'll apply and compare its hours with my repair roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for my household, with a long-running concern for the apprentices. Ten years is enough time to ask for conditions in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter about apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter that a line apprenticeship is worth considering if she can spend time on actual poles with a trained crew. I won't tell her every trade is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid instructor vacancy need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real instructor vacancy would have a full wage, regular hours and authority to stop unsafe practice. An occasional classroom visit would not replace my lead lineworker job. A classroom visit cannot replace a full power-line wage or teach an apprentice to stop unsafe work.

say: **Ten years** gives workers time to negotiate training before field robots arrive around 2039.
**2036 thinking AI** may change the office, but field safety instruction must remain.
think: A **full-wage instructor vacancy** could suit me at 56 if it actually opens.
Our **strong savings** let us wait for a real offer while paying the mortgage.
do: **Renew** line safety tickets and keep leading repair shifts.
**Review** apprentice field hours yearly through the union training committee.
**Apply** for a full-wage instructor opening if it includes real practice and stop authority.
feel: **Calm** about household options, with concern for apprentice opportunities.
S4.quote: A classroom visit cannot replace a full power-line wage or teach an apprentice to stop unsafe work.
fieldNote: His personal move remains **conditional** on a full paid instructor vacancy.
He continues **union monitoring** of field practice and paid apprentice hours across the decade.

steps.text: Renew line safety tickets and keep leading repair shifts
Review apprentice field hours yearly through union committee
Apply for full-wage instructor opening if real practice and stop authority included

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is little time before capable field robots arrive around 2031 and could reduce repair hours. A written crew plan and a negotiated pilot with paid observers and protected apprentice hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who trains the lineworkers after a robot takes the easy repair jobs. My family can lean on savings for a while, but a new apprentice needs real poles and paid time. I'd take that question to the union branch. My family can lean on savings for a while, but a new power-line apprentice needs real poles and paid time.

headlineQuote: My family can lean on savings for a while, but a new power-line apprentice needs real poles and paid time.
portrait: **Tomas**, 43, leads repairs on older electricity lines and brings high skill from a two-year technical diploma.
His **higher pay**, nine-month reserve, school-nurse partner and many nearby utility crews give his household options.
He has **never used AI** and presses for signed safety checks through his union branch.
As robots approach, he prioritises **paid apprentice practice** and would change roles only for a full-wage instructor vacancy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before field robots around 2031 might reduce repair hours.
whatWouldHelp: A written **crew plan** and negotiated pilot with paid observers and protected apprentice hours would help.
